Note that the “overprediction” of canopy cover by the UAS method compared to the field measurement increases as the tree density increases. Let’s look at that trend

# Data trends (dashed) are visualized using a LOESS (locally weighted scatterplot smoothing) regression. 
# A span of 1.0 was utilized to include 100% of the observations in each local neighborhood, 
# and the local polynomial degree was restricted to 1 (local linear regression) to prevent overfitting and boundary inflation at the data extremes.

# The dashed line represents a locally estimated scatterplot smoothing (LOESS) trend line
# , calculated with a smoothing parameter (span) of 1.0 and a local linear polynomial fit (degree = 1).
validation_plots_polygons %>%
  sf::st_drop_geometry() %>% 
  # dplyr::glimpse()
  ggplot2::ggplot(
    mapping = ggplot2::aes(y = diff_canopy_cov_pct, x = ref_trees_per_ha)
  ) + 
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "gray33", lwd = 1) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(color = "brown", alpha = 0.7, size = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::geom_smooth(
    method = "loess", se=F
    , span = 1 # 0.75 = default
    , method.args = list(degree = 1)
    , lwd = 1, color = "gray", linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  ggplot2::annotate(
    "text"
    , x = Inf
    # , y = 0.045
    , y = Inf
    , label = "prediction > reference"
    , hjust = 1.1
    , vjust = 1.2
    , parse = F
    , size = 2.5
  ) +
  ggplot2::annotate(
    "text"
    , x = Inf
    # , y = -0.04
    , y = -Inf
    , label = "prediction < reference"
    , hjust = 1.1
    , vjust = -0.4
    , parse = F
    , size = 2.5
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = scales::breaks_extended(n=8)) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(-1,1)
    # breaks = seq(-1,1,by=0.2)
    , breaks = scales::breaks_extended(n = 8)
    , labels = scales::percent
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "field reference TPH", y = "Canopy Cover difference"
    , subtitle = "Canopy Cover difference by reference TPH"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_light()

The higher canopy cover predictions by the UAS method compared to the field method is a logical outcome of how crown boundaries are defined by each method. The UAS approach delineates crowns from an aerial perspective and utilizes a segmentation routine that prevents any two crowns from overlapping. Conversely, the field method assumes a perfectly circular crown extending symmetrically from the tree stem. In dense stands, this circular geometry causes field-calculated crowns to overlap in 2D space which may artificially reduce the total canopy cover. In reality, tree branches grow asymmetrically. For example, extending away from competitors to capture available sunlight. The UAS captures this irregular, outward branch expansion which may explain why it results in larger (and more realistic) canopy cover measurements than the field-based method.

let’s check out a visual representation of that phenomenon by looking as some example plots after we define a plotting function

# harrypotter::hp(n=2, option="hermionegranger") %>% scales::show_col()
terra_plt_fn <- function(rgb, rgb_square, plot_poly, ref_pt, ref_poly, pred_poly, plot_title="", chm=NA) {
  grDevices::dev.new(canvas = "white")
  grDevices::dev.control("enable")
  
  if(inherits(chm,"SpatRaster")){
    terra::plotRGB(rgb, mar = c(0.2,0.2,1.2,3.2), bg = "white")
    # add chm
    terra::plot(
        chm
        , col = grDevices::hcl.colors(n = 100, palette = "YlGnBu") # viridis::plasma(n=100) # not good with the hermione orange
        # , col = grDevices::hcl.colors(n = 100, palette = "Purples")
        # , mar = c(b,l,t,r)
        , mar = c(0.2,0.2,1.2,3.2) 
        , bg = "white"
        , plg = list(
          title = "CHM (m)"
          , cex = 0.7, title.cex = 0.5, shrink = 0.7
        )
        , alpha = 0.4
        , add = T
      )
  }else{
    terra::plotRGB(rgb)
  }
  
  terra::plot(rgb_square, add = T, border = "white", col = NA, lwd = 2)
  
  terra::plot(terra::vect(plot_poly %>% sf::st_transform(terra::crs(rgb)) ), add = T, border = "white", col = NA, lwd = 0.8)
  terra::plot(terra::vect(ref_pt %>% sf::st_transform(terra::crs(rgb)) ), add = T, col = harrypotter::hp(n=2, option="hermionegranger")[1])
  terra::plot(terra::vect(ref_poly %>% sf::st_transform(terra::crs(rgb)) ), add = T, border = harrypotter::hp(n=2, option="hermionegranger")[1], col = NA, lwd = 1.4)
  terra::plot(terra::vect(pred_poly %>% sf::st_transform(terra::crs(rgb)) ), add = T, border = harrypotter::hp(n=2, option="hermionegranger")[2], col = NA, lwd = 1.4)
  # graphics::title(main = plot_title, cex.main = 0, col.main = "white", font.main = 2) 
  
  p <- grDevices::recordPlot()
  grDevices::dev.off()
  return(p)
}

# for a single record in the validation plot data
plt_validation_plots_polygons_fn <- function(x, addchm=F){
    # plot
    plot_temp <- validation_plots_polygons %>% dplyr::slice(x)
    # sq
    rgb_sq_temp <- plot_temp %>% 
      sf::st_buffer(1.5) %>% 
      sf::st_bbox() %>% 
      sf::st_as_sfc() %>% 
      sf::st_transform(terra::crs(rgb_rast)) %>% 
      terra::vect()
    # rgb
    rgb_temp <- rgb_rast %>% 
       terra::crop(
          rgb_sq_temp
        , mask=T
      )
    # ref pts
    ref_pt_temp <- validation_trees %>% dplyr::filter(plot==plot_temp$plot)
    # ref polys
    ref_poly_temp <- 
      ref_pt_temp %>% 
      dplyr::mutate(crown_radius_m=crown_diam_m/2) %>% 
      sf::st_buffer(.$crown_radius_m)
    # pred polys
    pred_poly_temp <- 
      crowns_sf %>% 
        dplyr::inner_join(
          treetops_sf %>% 
            dplyr::filter(
              tree_height_m>=min_tree_ht_m
              , dplyr::coalesce(inrange_th_votes,0)<=max_inrange_th_votes
            ) %>% 
            sf::st_intersection(plot_temp %>% sf::st_transform(sf::st_crs(treetops_sf)) ) %>% 
            sf::st_drop_geometry() %>% 
            dplyr::select(treeID)
          , by = "treeID"
        )
    # plt
    if(addchm){
      # rgb
      hey_chm <- chm_rast %>% 
         terra::crop(
            rgb_sq_temp
          , mask=T
        )
      plt <- terra_plt_fn(
        rgb = rgb_temp 
        , rgb_square = rgb_sq_temp 
        , plot_poly = plot_temp 
        , ref_pt = ref_pt_temp 
        , ref_poly = ref_poly_temp 
        , pred_poly = pred_poly_temp 
        , plot_title = paste0("plot: ",plot_temp$plot)
        , chm = hey_chm
      )
    }else{
      plt <- terra_plt_fn(
        rgb = rgb_temp 
        , rgb_square = rgb_sq_temp 
        , plot_poly = plot_temp 
        , ref_pt = ref_pt_temp 
        , ref_poly = ref_poly_temp 
        , pred_poly = pred_poly_temp 
        , plot_title = paste0("plot: ",plot_temp$plot)
      )
    }
    return(plt)
}

combine_validation_plots_polygons_fn <- function(plot_list,my_ncol=3) {
  n_plots <- length(plot_list)
  n_cols <- min(n_plots, my_ncol)
  n_rows <- ceiling(n_plots / n_cols)
  
  grob_list <- purrr::map(plot_list, cowplot::as_grob)
  
  # grDevices::dev.new()
  cowplot::plot_grid(
    plotlist = grob_list
    , ncol = n_cols
    , nrow = n_rows
  )  
  # graphics::par(mfrow = c(n_rows, n_cols), mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))
  #   for (i in seq_len(n_plots)) {
  #   grDevices::replayPlot(plot_list[[i]])
  # }
}

interesting. we see that the UAS crowns (orange) generally align with the green areas that appear to be trees from the aerial perspective and the individual crowns segmented using the UAS method do not overlap. By contrast, the field-measured stems and the assumed circular crowns (red) overlap with each other and are not always spatially aligned with the green areas in the aerial imagery. This slight misalignment is the result of variations in the location recording systems used on the ground and the UAS in addition to the stems of trees not being positioned directly under the crown due to real-world tree lean. We can also see a few examples of field-measured tree stems that are very near each other so that the simulated circular crowns have high or even complete overlap.

4.9.1.1 Crown IoU

We can move beyond summary canopy cover percentages and evaluate the spatial overlap of the crown footprints using the Intersection over Union (IoU) metric. The IoU index provides a spatial assessment by measuring the geographic alignment between the UAS crown polygons and circular field crowns. To quantify the spatial agreement between your UAS-delineated crowns and the field-calculated circular crowns, IoU is calculated by dividing the area of overlap between the two crown layers by the total combined area of both layers:

\[ \text{IoU}=\frac{\text{Area of Intersection}}{\text{Area of Union}}=\frac{|A\cap B|}{|A\cup B|} \]

where \(A\) represents the spatial footprint of the field-calculated circular crowns within a plot and \(B\) represents the spatial footprint of the UAS-segmented crown polygons within the same plot.

# validation_plots_polygons %>% dplyr::glimpse()
iou_temp <-
  1:nrow(validation_plots_polygons) %>% 
  purrr::map(function(x){
    # warning(x, immediate. = T)
    # plot
    plot_temp <- validation_plots_polygons %>% dplyr::slice(x)
    # ref polys
    if(any(sf::st_is_empty(plot_temp$ref_canopy_cov_geom))){
      return(
        plot_temp %>% 
          sf::st_drop_geometry() %>% 
          dplyr::select(plot) %>% 
          dplyr::mutate(
            crown_pred_ref_iou = as.numeric(NA)
          )
      )
    }
    ref_poly_temp <- 
      plot_temp$ref_canopy_cov_geom %>% 
      sf::st_transform(sf::st_crs(treetops_sf)) %>% 
      sf::st_union()
    
    # pred polys
    if(any(sf::st_is_empty(plot_temp$pred_canopy_cov_geom))){
      return(
        plot_temp %>% 
          sf::st_drop_geometry() %>% 
          dplyr::select(plot) %>% 
          dplyr::mutate(
            crown_pred_ref_iou = 0
          )
      )
    }
    pred_poly_temp <- 
      plot_temp$pred_canopy_cov_geom %>% 
      sf::st_transform(sf::st_crs(treetops_sf)) %>% 
      sf::st_union()
    
    u <- sf::st_union(ref_poly_temp,pred_poly_temp)
    i <- sf::st_intersection(ref_poly_temp,pred_poly_temp)
    
    # terra::plot(u, col = "gray88", border = "gray88", lwd = 10)
    # terra::plot(ref_poly_temp, col = NA, border = "firebrick", lwd = 4, add = T)
    # terra::plot(pred_poly_temp, col = NA, border = "orange", lwd = 4, add = T)
    
    if(length(i)==0){
      return(
        plot_temp %>% 
          sf::st_drop_geometry() %>% 
          dplyr::select(plot) %>% 
          dplyr::mutate(
            crown_pred_ref_iou = 0
          )
      )  
    }
    
    return(
      plot_temp %>% 
        sf::st_drop_geometry() %>% 
        dplyr::select(plot) %>% 
        dplyr::mutate(
          crown_pred_ref_iou = as.numeric(sf::st_area(i))/as.numeric(sf::st_area(u))
        )
    )
  }) %>% 
  purrr::list_rbind()
# iou_temp %>% dplyr::glimpse()
# add
validation_plots_polygons <- validation_plots_polygons %>% dplyr::left_join(iou_temp, by = "plot")

4.9.2 Plot Height Evaluation

In addition to canopy cover and as part of our plot-level evaluation of the UAS tree detection methodology, we’ll also evaluate mean tree height at the plot level to validate the vertical profile representation of the UAS data. We’ll calculate these plot-level metrics by aggregating tree-level UAS predictions and field-reference values irrespective of individual instance matching. Following the terminology established by Li (2009), plot tree height is defined as the average height of individual trees within a plot boundary. While Li (2009) used a diameter threshold of at least 5 inches DBH to calcuate plot tree height, we used a tree height threshold of 2 m applied to both the UAS and field trees.

cc_agg_temp <- validation_plots_polygons %>%
  # dplyr::group_by(trtmnt_type) %>%
  get_me_rmse_fn()

# get the plottttttttttttttttttt
validation_plots_polygons %>%
  sf::st_drop_geometry() %>%
  dplyr::bind_cols(
    cc_agg_temp
  ) %>%
  plt_scatter_fn(which_col = "mean_tree_height_m", title_lab = "plot tree height", x_lab = "reference plot tree height (m)", y_lab = "predicted plot tree height (m)")

The aggregation comparing the plot tree height of the field method to the UAS method yielded an RMSE of 0.67 and a mean error (ME) of -0.25. These values mean that the average UAS prediction of plot tree height is off by about ±0.67 meters from the field-measured value which is generally considered highly accurate and operationally acceptable. The negative ME of -0.25 means that, on average across all plots, the UAS method is systematically underpredicting plot tree height by 0.25 meters compared to the field data.

we can table the plot tree height measurement aggregated over all field plots

# Data trends (dashed) are visualized using a LOESS (locally weighted scatterplot smoothing) regression. 
# A span of 1.0 was utilized to include 100% of the observations in each local neighborhood, 
# and the local polynomial degree was restricted to 1 (local linear regression) to prevent overfitting and boundary inflation at the data extremes.

# The dashed line represents a locally estimated scatterplot smoothing (LOESS) trend line

it appears that one of the primary problems with the UAS plot tree height measurements in these plots with the largest disagreement between the field and UAS plot tree height measurements is due to the UAS method segmenting more, smaller trees than were measured in the field. The average number of trees counted by the UAS method in these example plots is 4.8 compared to an average of 2.8 trees counted in the field.

the UAS is oversegmenting trees in these plots, possibly splitting a single, actual tree into multiple segments due to the common growth form in pinyon-juniper systems where trees may have weak apical dominance and lack a single, strict leader. let’s see if we can visualize this using the CHM data

# # good example of multiple potential leaders visible in the shadow 
# # that the UAS splits into 4 trees but the field measured 1 tree
# plt_validation_plots_polygons_fn(1,addchm = T)
plts_temp <- 
  validation_plots_polygons %>% 
  dplyr::mutate(rn = dplyr::row_number()) %>% 
  dplyr::filter(plot %in% unique(ht_huh_temp$plot)) %>% 
  dplyr::pull(rn) %>% 
  purrr::map(
    \(x)
    plt_validation_plots_polygons_fn(x,addchm = T)    
  )
plt_temp <- combine_validation_plots_polygons_fn(plts_temp,my_ncol = 4)
cowplot::save_plot(
  filename = "../data/field_uas_crown_treeht_comp.png"
  , plot = plt_temp 
  , base_width = 10.5
  , base_height = 7
  , ncol = 1
  , nrow = 1
  , dpi = 300
  , bg = "white"
)
print(plt_temp)

there are a lot of things going on in those example plots and it does not appear that the primary issue is the UAS oversegmenting larger trees with mulitple possible leaders, though that is the case in a few of the examples. Other discrepancies include plot edge effects influencing which trees were determined to be “in” the plot, a few cases of undersegmentation by the UAS, standing dead trees not removed by the RGB spectral filter applied at the very beginning of this section, potential “missed” trees in the field plot data (or these trees were not included in the validation data due to not meeting the 2 m minimum tree height threshold or were removed due to other missing data like missing coordinates). Either way, the tendency of the UAS method to underpredict height at the upper-limit of plot tree height does not appear to be systematically due to a single factor.
